description: I'm Pratt, a final-year Computer Science (AI) student at Swinburne, Melbourne. My skills include Python, machine learning, cloud systems and full-stack development. For Flame in Freefall, I want to turn NASA fire research into a trustworthy AI tool benefiting space and Earth. I'm seeking teammates in data science, combustion science, UI/UX, visualisation or storytelling. Join me to learn, build a polished demo and compete seriously while having fun!
summary:
FlameBound helps spacecraft and habitat engineers see where NASA's microgravity fire evidence applies to the air they are designing for, and where it stops. An engineer picks a cabin atmosphere (ISS, lunar base, exploration cabin or EVA suit), an airflow and a material. FlameBound then finds the closest test among NASA's 23 open PSI combustion investigations, scores the match with a transparent Boundary Condition Match Score, and shows NASA's original values, the differences from the target, and the DOI. Where the match is weak it warns instead of guessing, and a short AI briefing, checked automatically for citations and numbers, explains the gap in plain English.

What it found: in the NASA PSI records we ingested, today's ISS cabin air has a close test for 8 of 8 common materials (4 on the exact material), but the Moon-base, exploration and EVA atmospheres have one for 0 of 24 material and atmosphere combinations. NASA's solid-material tests that recorded oxygen ran at 13.6% to 22.2%, and none recorded pressure.

This matters because lunar habitats are expected to use oxygen-rich air, where materials burn more easily. FlameBound makes NASA's fire data searchable by design conditions and shows engineers which evidence to seek next. It does not say whether a material is safe.
details:
What it does

FlameBound is a web tool for spacecraft and habitat engineers. They choose a cabin atmosphere (ISS, lunar base, exploration cabin or EVA suit, or their own oxygen, pressure and airflow), a material, a gravity level and a question (flammability, suppression or detection). FlameBound finds the closest test among NASA's 23 open PSI combustion investigations and returns a transparent Boundary Condition Match Score (BCMS), NASA's original values beside each converted value, the differences from the target, and the DOI. A hazard warning appears when the best match scores below 65%, was tested more than 2 percentage points of oxygen away, or when Moon or Mars gravity is selected. FlameBound matches conditions and names only. It does not say whether a material is safe.

Try it in the live app. ISS cabin air, SIBAL fabric, 20 cm/s: close NASA coverage (84%). Lunar base air, PMMA, 5 cm/s: hazard warning (best match 60.1%).

Also in the app: an Evidence Gap Atlas (4 atmospheres x 8 materials x 2 airflows, 64 cells, CSV export); a Materials checker (paste a list of materials; it stays in the browser); Ask NASA (answers only from 193 passages of the 23 investigations, every sentence cites a passage, quotes must match NASA's words, and it declines off-topic questions); a printable evidence report; and a validation panel that re-runs 7 acceptance scenarios live in the browser.

What it found

In the NASA PSI records FlameBound ingested, today's ISS cabin air has a close test for 8 of 8 common materials (4 on the exact material, 4 through a different solid). The Moon-base, exploration-cabin and EVA-suit atmospheres have one for 0 of 24 material and atmosphere combinations, at each airflow setting. These are classifications under FlameBound's matching rules, not safety findings. NASA's solid-material tests that recorded oxygen ran at 13.6% to 22.2%, and none recorded pressure.

How it works

1) A Python pipeline pulls 23 combustion investigations and their tables from NASA's PSI repository, converts every condition to common units, and gives each value a status (recorded, approximate, range, not recorded and so on). That produces 1,980 records.

2) In the browser, BCMS is a fixed weighted sum over what NASA recorded: oxygen 30%, material 25%, airflow 20%, pressure 15%, pillar and scale 10%. A condition NASA did not record contributes zero, with no re-weighting and no guessing.

3) An AI model (Claude Haiku 5.5 in the live app) writes a short briefing from an evidence pack. Automated checks require each sentence to cite evidence, every number to appear in it, and no safety verdicts. If a check fails there is one retry, then a labelled plain fallback. The AI never ranks or scores.

Benefits

Engineers see in seconds which NASA tests are closest to their conditions, and exactly where the evidence stops. Example: lunar-base air (30% O2) with PMMA at 5 cm/s airflow is not closely covered. The best match, SAFFIRE-II 2-7, scores 60.1%, was run 7.9 percentage points of oxygen away, and did not record pressure. FlameBound makes that gap visible instead of letting results from other conditions be read as if they applied.

Testing

95 automated tests; 7 of 7 acceptance scenarios; the top match is unchanged in 58 of 60 weight changes; 11 of 12 Ask NASA questions answered with a correct source and 3 of 3 off-topic questions declined (our own small development set); 0 axe accessibility violations in the tested views. No independent combustion or spacecraft-safety specialist has reviewed the matching yet.

Limits

The BCMS weights and the 65% and 2-point thresholds are our design choices and have not been independently validated. A match through a different solid may not reflect how the target material behaves. The 0 of 24 result holds under FlameBound's matching rules and the records we ingested. It does not mean NASA has no relevant experiments elsewhere. A combustion specialist should review all three before anyone relies on the results.

Self-audit and baseline check (ours, not independent)

We re-checked the top match for all 7 acceptance scenarios against NASA's original table rows. The record ID, material, oxygen and airflow cells match NASA's text exactly in 7 of 7. The SAFFIRE-I, SAFFIRE-II, SAFFIRE-III and BASS-II tables have no pressure column, and FLEX test 42's 535 mmHg converts to 71.3 kPa. The solid-material oxygen range of 13.6% to 22.2% was confirmed in the BASS-II table; the BASS table was not re-checked. We also compared FlameBound with a simple baseline (exact material, then nearest oxygen). Across the 64 Evidence Gap Atlas cells the two give the same coverage label in 56. They agree on all 48 Moon-base, exploration and EVA cells (every one a gap), and differ only on 8 ISS cells (Kapton, Teflon, Pyrell foam and lampwick at two airflows), where FlameBound accepts a similar solid and the baseline does not. So the 0 of 24 result does not depend on BCMS's extra scoring. This comparison does not show whether that extra scoring helps engineers.

What we hope to achieve

A trusted first stop for fire-safety evidence during habitat and rover design, and a clear view of which atmospheres, airflows and materials still need microgravity or partial-gravity testing.

Tools

Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS (web app, hosted on Vercel); Python (data pipeline); Node test runner and GitHub Actions CI; Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Anthropic API for the briefing. Open source under Apache-2.0. All data is NASA PSI (CC0).

Use of AI (SI)

Prattay Banik decided what to build and the architecture, and approved the changes. Claude (Anthropic) wrote most of the code and helped draft the text. Codex (OpenAI) independently reviewed the plan and app and wrote the explanation and numeric-check hardening. In the live app, Claude Haiku 5.5 drafts the short briefings, each labelled SI-generated. SI was not used to come up with the idea. The demo slides use real screenshots; there are no AI-generated images, video, voice or music, and no AI-generated data values.
